extracted.intended_audience: eighteenth-century literate public: writers, artists, composers, and tradesmen interested in taste and public display
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and aesthetic rules for public inscriptions, monuments, shop-signs, and musical composition — arguing that public art should suit national language and taste. Applies to designers of monuments and shop signs, composers and dramatists, and cultural critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs should do more than record birth/death
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitaphs that only record that a person 'was born upon one Day and died upon another' reduce a life to those two common circumstances and become a kind of satiric register of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to commemorate deeds, character, or thoughtfulness rather than only dates; avoid turning monuments into mere registers. Anti-pattern: tombs that 'recorded nothing else of the buried Person, but that he was born upon one Day and died upon another.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscriptions and public monuments should be vetted by learned/tasteful critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Public monuments and inscriptions are a nation's public face and should be 'submitted to the Perusal of Men of Learning and Genius before they are put in Execution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have inscriptions and monument designs reviewed for elegance and justness of thought to ensure they reflect national politeness and literacy. This prevents ignorant or offensive displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monuments must represent the true character and deeds of the person
rubrics_metrics.description: A monument should reflect the distinguishing character and notable actions of the deceased rather than an inappropriate or fashionable image (e.g., a rough admiral represented as a beau).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose imagery and inscription that celebrates real achievements and character. Anti-pattern: Sir Cloudesly Shovel depicted 'by the Figure of a Beau, dress'd in a long Perriwig' and an inscription celebrating only the 'Manner of his Death' instead of his services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use profession-appropriate symbols and ornaments on monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments of public servants (e.g., admirals) should be adorned with truthful, profession-related symbolism (rostral crowns, naval ornaments, festoons of seaweed, shells, coral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match symbolic ornamentation to the person's life and profession so the monument communicates meaning at a glance; model good taste as observed in Dutch public monuments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscure languages on public inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessively modest inscriptions written in Greek or Hebrew may be unintelligible to the public ('not understood once in a Twelve-month').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer language accessible to intended readers; inscriptions should communicate rather than signal erudition. Anti-pattern: tomb inscriptions deliberately or negligently unreadable to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop signs should bear affinity to the wares they advertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Every shop should make use of a sign which bears some affinity to the Wares in which it deals; it is inconsistent, for example, 'to see a Bawd at the Sign of the Angel, or a Taylor at the Lion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sign imagery that relates to the trade (tools, products, or trade-related symbols). Anti-patterns: goat before a perfumer, the French King's Head at a sword-cutler's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jarring, incongruous, or monster combinations on signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit creatures of 'jarring and incongruous Natures' joined together on the same sign (e.g., the Bell and the Neats-tongue, the Dog and Gridiron; flying Pigs, Hogs in Armour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure visual coherence and natural association in sign composition; clear the streets of 'Monsters' and bizarre pairings that confuse meaning. Exception: long-established conceits (e.g., Cat and Fiddle) may be retained if understood as a conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit quartering/borrowing of other trades' signs
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be rules determining how far one tradesman may 'give' the Sign of another and in what cases he may 'quarter' it with his own, since copying masters' signs has produced many absurdities (e.g., 'three Nuns and a Hare').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clear conventions for when a business may display another's device (heritage, apprenticeship), otherwise avoid composite quarterings that produce incoherent signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use name-based/punning devices thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proprietor's name suggests a device (Mrs. Salmon with a trout, Mr. Bell displaying a bell), using it is an opportunity to 'let the World know who he is' and to create clever, intelligible signage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit nominative devices for clarity and wit; they can generate public amusement and recognition (examples: Abel Drugger, the Bell-Savage). But ensure the pun/device remains intelligible and tasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs convey the temperament of the inhabitant
rubrics_metrics.description: One can 'give a shrewd Guess at the Humour of the Inhabitant by the Sign' (e.g., a 'surly cholerick Fellow generally makes Choice of a Bear; as Men of milder Dispositions, frequently live at the Lamb').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select signage consistent with the proprietor's character or the desired public persona; misaligned signage may mislead or create ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitative music must suit the accent and tone of the language performed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cadences and accent of recitative are tied to the native 'Tone or Accent' of each language; therefore 'the Recitative Musick in every Language, should be as different as the Tone or Accent of each Language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or setting recitative, adapt cadences and prosody to match the natural spoken accent of the language — do not rigidly apply Italian recitative to English words. Anti-pattern: English words set to Italian recitative causing audiences to misread questions as anger or quarrels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt foreign musical elements to native genius rather than replacing it
rubrics_metrics.description: Composers may borrow graces from other national styles (e.g., Italian graces), but should not 'entirely annihilate and destroy' their native music; the infusion should 'Civilize' or 'cultivate' rather than supplant the local tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate useful foreign techniques selectively to soften and embellish native music, while preserving what fits the people's genius (Lully's cultivation of French music from Italian graces given as a positive example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's rules should be deduced from popular taste, not vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Musick, Architecture, Painting, Poetry, and Oratory 'are to deduce their Laws and Rules from the general Sense and Taste of Mankind, and not from the Principles of those Arts themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create works that respond to the audience's perceptions and sensibilities rather than imposing esoteric art-theory; art should accommodate common ears/eyes and distinguish harsh from disagreeable notes accessible to ordinary judges.
